title: McCulloch and Pitts: Modeling a Neuron as Logic (1943)
explainer: Years before Rosenblatt's perceptron, neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch and logician Walter Pitts published a 1943 paper arguing that networks of simplified, all-or-nothing neurons could in principle compute any function expressible in propositional logic. Their model never learned from data at all - its weights were fixed by hand - but it's the reason a 'neuron' in these diagrams is drawn as weighted inputs feeding a threshold, a convention that predates any trainable network by over a decade.

title: Backpropagation Was Discovered Several Times Before It Stuck
explainer: The backpropagation algorithm used to train the networks in this lesson wasn't invented once: the core trick of applying the chain rule backward through a computation was described in Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 thesis and worked out independently by others through the 1970s, yet it only became the standard way to train multi-layer networks after Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams's widely read 1986 paper. The gap between a technique existing and a field actually adopting it is itself a useful thing to notice as a self-taught learner.
